text:
Help me write a cover letter. I've taught high school chemistry for 9 years and I'm applying to be a training coordinator at a pharmaceutical manufacturing plant about 30 minutes from me.

About me:
- I teach about 140 students a year across five classes.
- I wrote our school's lab safety program in 2019. Since then we've had no injuries in our labs that needed more than first aid.
- Our AP Chemistry pass rate went from 41% to 58% over the four years I've taught the course.
- Every year I train our new science teachers on lab procedures, about 12 hours each. There have been two a year on average.
- I've never worked in a regulated industry. The job posting asks for experience with GMP training records, which I don't have.
- I use Google Classroom. The plant uses a learning management system I haven't used.

I want the letter to say I can cut their new-hire training time in half. One page.

Before I draft this, I have a few questions. Your answers will change what the letter says.

1. **What's behind "cut new-hire training time in half"?** Do you know how long their onboarding takes now, or have you shortened a training program yourself before? As written, it's a promise about a plant you haven't seen. A hiring manager in a regulated industry may read it as not understanding why GMP training takes as long as it does. If you have something concrete behind it, I'll build the claim around that. If not, I'd suggest offering to make new hires competent faster and more consistently, backed by your lab-safety record and your onboarding of new teachers. Which do you want?
2. **What's the company, and who should the letter go to?** Also tell me the job title exactly as posted, and paste the main requirements if you can. Then I can match their wording and pick which of your results to lead with.
3. **Have you done anything to close the GMP gap?** For example, a GMP or FDA 21 CFR Part 11 course, reading their LMS vendor's documentation, or talking to someone at the plant. Even one step lets the letter take on that gap directly instead of leaving it as a question.
4. **Why this move, and why now?** One honest sentence about why you're leaving teaching for manufacturing training helps the reader trust the rest.
5. **What did the lab safety program actually involve?** For example, written procedures, sign-offs, refresher schedules, records of who was trained on what. If you kept documentation like that, it's the closest thing you have to GMP training records, and I'd put it front and center.

1. I don't know how long their training takes now. What I have done is rewrite our new-teacher lab training in 2020, which took it from 20 hours to 12. I'm fine with saying that instead of promising to cut theirs in half.

2. It's Calder Pharmaceuticals, the plant in Westfield. The posting names Karen Doyle as the HR manager. I don't have the exact job title or the full requirements list in front of me.

3. Yes, I've enrolled in an online GMP basics course. It finishes May 2.

4. I don't have an answer for that one yet.

5. I keep a signed training record for every new teacher I train and for every student's lab safety quiz. The state has audited our lab safety records twice and found nothing.

I wrote the letter around the 20-to-12-hour rewrite instead of a promise about their training. I also named the GMP gap directly and paired it with your course.

[Your Name]
[Street Address]
[City, State ZIP]
[Phone] · [Email]

[Date]

Karen Doyle
HR Manager
Calder Pharmaceuticals
Westfield, [State]

Dear Ms. Doyle,

I am applying for the Training Coordinator position at Calder Pharmaceuticals' Westfield plant. I have taught high school chemistry for nine years. Much of that work has been what a manufacturing plant relies on: teaching people to handle hazardous materials safely and the same way every time, and keeping records that show who was trained on what.

In 2019 I wrote our school's lab safety program. It now covers about 140 students a year across five classes. Since it began, we have had no lab injury that needed more than first aid. I keep a signed training record for every student's safety quiz and for every new teacher I train. The state has audited those records twice and found nothing.

Every year I also train our new science teachers on lab procedures, about two people a year. In 2020 I rewrote that training and cut it from 20 hours to 12. At Calder I would take the same approach: work out what a new hire needs to do the job correctly and safely, then teach exactly that, clearly and in order.

I can also show that my teaching gets results. Over the four years I have taught AP Chemistry, our pass rate rose from 41% to 58%.

I have not worked in a regulated industry, and I have not kept GMP training records. To close that gap, I have enrolled in a GMP basics course that I will finish on May 2. I have run my classes through Google Classroom for years. I have not used the learning management system your plant uses, and I would make learning it one of my first priorities.

I live about 30 minutes from the Westfield plant and would welcome the chance to talk about how I could help your team train new hires well. Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]
</final_document>

A few notes:

- **Job title:** I used "Training Coordinator." Check it against the exact title in the posting, and add the plant's state to the address block.
- **Why you're changing careers:** The letter doesn't explain this. That's fine for now, but an interviewer is likely to ask, so it's worth having a sentence ready. If you come up with one, it could go at the end of the first paragraph.
- **Length:** The letter is about 370 words, so it will fit on one page with a standard header.
